source.id: TITLE:Dropout: a simple way to prevent neural networks from overfitting
source.title: Dropout: a simple way to prevent neural networks from overfitting
source.authors: Nitish Srivastava; Geoffrey Hinton; Alex Krizhevsky; Ilya Sutskever; Ruslan Salakhutdinov

record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own comparisons of dropout and no-dropout models, including outcomes on natural-label held-out sets, but does not test random-label memorization or the claim’s other central interventions.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper’s dropout-versus-no-dropout comparisons and its reported dropout-rate and dataset-size sweeps. Comparisons with other regularizers and the autoencoder feature observations are not extracted because they do not directly measure a listed version’s named outcome. Results attributed to cited prior studies are not included.
record.test_reason: This is the original V6 study. It directly compares held-out performance with and without dropout and tests dependence on training-set size and retention probability. It does not test V1–V5, V7 or V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate: authors conclude that dropout improves generalization across multiple application domains, with benefits depending on dataset size and retention probability. They report typically two to three times longer training for the same architecture. The proposed co-adaptation mechanism is their explanation, rather than a separately established cause.
record.recipe_differences: The paper directly applies dropout training and compares against no-dropout baselines, but the catalog claim concerns broad generalization behavior and this original study does not test the claim’s random-label, width-threshold, optimizer, batch-size, sharpness or memorized-example formulations.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset size and dropout retention probability change the reported outcome; dropout location changes SVHN results, and on CIFAR-100 the fully-connected-only dropout result is better than dropout in all layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Alternative-splicing dropout networks achieve 567 bits of Code Quality versus 440 for a cited early-stopped neural network.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dropout can improve held-out predictive distribution quality on alternative-splicing tasks.

record.problems: Many comparisons are not matched for architecture or recipe; some comparisons are to prior published systems. Several figure-based sweeps have no numerical values in text. No uncertainty estimates are given for most classification results. TIMIT text and table differ on the 8-layer pretrained comparator (20.5% versus 20.7%).
record.rows_left_out: No required V6 dropout outcomes omitted. Other regularizer comparisons in Table 9, autoencoder feature visualizations and sparsity measurements are not rows for the listed versions; ImageNet and other listed dropout scores without matched no-dropout comparisons are retained only as context rows where reported.

untested.parts: Coexistence of natural-label generalization and random-label fitting, including chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Width beyond the interpolation threshold under convergence without explicit regularization; dropout width comparisons do not test this.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers and tuning-dependent generalization.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Joint removal of dropout and weight decay with data augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness rankings and generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

missing.what: Matched MNIST comparisons across six architectures: two, three and four hidden layers with 1024 or 2048 units. Authors report substantially lower test errors with dropout across all architectures using fixed hyperparameters.
MNIST dropout with ReLUs obtains 1.25% error, separating the activation change from the subsequent max-norm improvement to 1.06%.
Pretrained MNIST comparisons: DBN fine-tuning error falls from 1.18% to 0.92% with dropout; DBM fine-tuning error falls from 0.96% to 0.79%. Baseline scores are attributed to prior publications.

The training-size sweep also includes 1K, 5K, 10K and 50K examples. Authors report that dropout gains increase and then decline as training-set size grows; only the two smallest conditions are recorded.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels are issued because this study is an original source for V6. Small-data non-improvement and excessive-dropout underfitting are already explicit parts of V6. Table 9 was declared omitted, so it is not listed as an undeclared missing result; nevertheless, its same-architecture comparisons directly bear on V6: L2 versus dropout plus L2 gives 1.62% versus 1.25%, and max-norm versus dropout plus max-norm gives 1.35% versus 1.05%. The record's claim that these comparisons do not measure a listed version is incorrect.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and test performance; natural-label generalization under standard training without dropout.
Width sweep beyond the zero-training-error threshold without explicit regularization.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizers and their held-out performance.
Large versus small batch training under fixed epoch budgets.

The paper does not report dropout outcomes on very small training sets of size 100 or 500 as a distinct held-out error comparison; it states dropout gives no improvement there. It does not test jointly removing dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples and comparing with random-example removal.

rows.subject: neural net
rows.operation_detail: Train on MNIST without dropout; compare with dropout NN.
rows.note: The cited standard neural net result is described as a best result without dropout or unsupervised pretraining; no matched architecture or recipe is specified for comparison.
rows.check: Cited comparator from Simard et al. (2003), not this study's experiment. Table 2 specifies two layers of 800 logistic units, not three layers of 1024 units. Retain only as attributed baseline context.

rows.note: Text says dropout reduces error from about 1.60% to 1.35%.
rows.check: The 1.35% result uses logistic units and is compared with a cited, differently sized network at 1.60%; this is not a matched dropout ablation.

rows.subject: Dropout NN + max-norm constraint
rows.operation_detail: Train with dropout and max-norm constraint.
rows.baseline: 1.60% for best networks without dropout or unsupervised pretraining
rows.note: This comparison combines dropout with max-norm regularization.
rows.check: The 1.06% model uses ReLUs as well as max-norm regularization. The closer preceding comparison is 1.25% for dropout with ReLUs; the reduction from 1.60% combines several changes.

rows.note: The text says this large network generalizes despite having more than 65 million parameters, but no matched no-dropout result for this architecture is provided.
rows.check: Correct standalone score, but no matched no-dropout baseline establishes the dropout effect for this architecture.

rows.subject: Dropout NN
rows.operation_detail: Train with dropout while varying retention probability at fixed architecture.
rows.value: Test error falls as p increases, is flat for 0.4 ≤ p ≤ 0.8, then increases near 1; exact values figure only
rows.note: The prose states low p leads to underfitting; larger p improves error until a flat region, then error increases as p approaches 1.
rows.check: Correct the size to three hidden layers of 2048 units. The sweep demonstrates V6's stated excessive-dropout underfitting condition; split low-retention underfitting from intermediate-retention improvement rather than assigning one partial state to the whole sweep.

rows.baseline: For p = 0.1 error fell from 2.7% to 1.7% compared with fixed-width setting
rows.value: Values of p close to 0.6 seem to perform best; exact curve figure only
rows.note: Paper says errors for small p are much reduced compared with fixed width, and p near 0.6 seems best.
rows.check: The 2.7% to 1.7% comparison changes network width at fixed p=0.1, rather than adding dropout to a fixed network. Record it as a width-by-rate interaction; the aggregate row lacks a readable no-dropout comparison.
